1.pericope_label: Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that entereth not by the door into the sheepfold, but climbeth up some other way, the same is a thief and a robber. But he that entereth in by the door is the shepherd of the sheep. To him the porter openeth; and the sheep hear his voice: and he calleth his own sheep by name, and leadeth them out. And when he putteth forth his own sheep, he goeth before them, and the sheep follow him: for they know his voice. And a stranger will they not follow, but will flee from him: for they know not the voice of strangers. This parable spake Jesus unto them: but they understood not what things they were which he spake unto them.

schools.summary: Barnes argues from the formula, since the doubled asseveration is never used to open a discourse, so that the words follow straight on from the charge of blindness laid against men claiming to be shepherds; he applies the door narrowly to the ministry, the Pharisees having claimed the pastoral office without the appointment that alone opens it, and observes that in every church many have sought that office from ambition or love of ease. Ellicott raises a question of method before the details are pressed, since the word used is not the ordinary word for parable but a wider one covering any figurative speech, and in a parable the outer story is kept distinct from the truth it carries while here form and idea interpenetrate; he concludes that every particular, the porter expressly, is not to be pressed. Lightfoot alone describes the thing itself, the pen where the flock was gathered at night and the lambs tithed, the little door at which two could not pass together, the tenth lamb marked with red; and he supplies the legal distinction the terms carry, a thief taking when the owner is not privy and a robber openly and by force, the same line Barnes draws between stealth and bloodshed.
Clarke reports both datings without choosing, one putting the discourse immediately after the last and the other three months later.

Henry leaves the dating open, noting that the later mention of the winter feast may date what precedes as well as what follows, the sheep metaphor being still in use when that feast is named. On the shepherd walking ahead he answers from custom rather than from doctrine, that going before was the way of the country, the shepherd walking first to meet danger.

Chrysostom presses the particulars the other way. The porter he suggests is Moses, as the man to whom the oracles of God were committed; the door is the Scriptures, which admit us to the knowledge of God and bar the entrance to heretics, so that climbing another way means a self-chosen path, or the traditions of men taught to the neglect of the Law, and the verb is not entering but climbing, like a thief going over a wall. He resolves the shifting figure by office: bringing us to the Father he is the door, caring for us the shepherd. He also holds that shepherds always go behind their flocks and that this one goes before, which is the point.

Augustine offers the Lord himself as the porter, since there is far less distance between a door and a porter than between a door and a shepherd, and he has already called himself both; if another person is wanted, take the Spirit who guides into all truth, but never esteem the porter greater than the door. He turns the verse against respectable unbelief, since many pass for good men by the world's measure and keep the Law after a fashion without being Christians, and a good life profits only as it leads to life eternal. He adds the image the others lack, that Christ is a lowly door and whoever would come through with his head whole must stoop; and he will not tidy away the difficulty that sometimes those who are not sheep hear the voice, since the traitor heard it, and sometimes the sheep do not, since some who crucified him were his sheep.

debates.question: Who is the porter that opens to the shepherd?

positions.position: Moses, as the man to whom the oracles of God were committed
The Lord himself, or else the Spirit who guides into all truth, but never anyone esteemed greater than the door
Not to be identified at all, since this is not strictly a parable and its particulars are not to be pressed

debates.question: Does the discourse continue the preceding scene or open a new occasion?

positions.position: It continues it, since the doubled asseveration is never used to begin a discourse
Left open, the winter feast named later possibly dating what precedes as well as what follows
Both datings reported, one immediately after the last discourse and one three months later

debates.question: Why is it remarked that the shepherd goes before the sheep?

positions.position: Because it reverses the usual practice, shepherds going behind their flocks
Because it was the custom of that country, the shepherd walking ahead to meet danger

outliers.claim: Alone describes the fold as a working pen, with its two doors, the nightly gathering and daily milking, and the tithing of lambs counted out and marked with red while the ewes waited outside.
Refuses to smooth the figure, granting that some who are not sheep hear the voice, the traitor having heard it, and that some who are sheep do not, since some who crucified him were his own.

But he that entereth in by the door is the shepherd of the sheep.
To him the porter openeth; and the sheep hear his voice: and he calleth his own sheep by name, and leadeth them out.

This parable spake Jesus unto them: but they understood not what things they were which he spake unto them.

7.pericope_label: Then said Jesus unto them again, Verily, verily, I say unto you, I am the door of the sheep. All that ever came before me are thieves and robbers: but the sheep did not hear them. I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved, and shall go in and out, and find pasture. The thief cometh not, but for to steal, and to kill, and to destroy: I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly.

schools.summary: Lightfoot would gladly have referred the words to men who had claimed the title of Messiah and imposed themselves on the people, except that he can find hardly a single instance of anyone doing so before the true Messiah came, whereas after that coming there were a great many; he treats the asymmetry as evidence that the moment when Jesus appeared was precisely the moment the nation was looking for the Messiah, and supplies a drier note from the rabbis, who fixed the distance a beast might go out to pasture at sixteen miles. Barnes reaches the same conclusion independently and settles on the scribes and Pharisees as the men meant, disarming the word all as used in the popular sense the New Testament often gives it; on the last clause he distinguishes bare existence from the abundance superadded to it. Ellicott sets the saying beside the strait gate and the narrow way and draws the line firmly in both directions, that no shepherd enters the fold except through the character and life and death of Christ, and that we may neither narrow that door nor widen it; the fold, he adds, stands always open to the man who came in by it.

Gill works through the exceptions: not Moses, not the prophets of the Lord, not the Baptist who prepared the way, but those who came unsent, and the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves; he adds a particular identification, the three shepherds cut off in one month, which he takes for the three sects and their leaders. On the other side of the contrast he describes the thief's aim, to carry the sheep away from their shepherd and steal their hearts as a rebel prince once stole the hearts of a kingdom from his father.

Clarke takes going in and out as a Hebrew idiom covering the whole activity of a life and the liberty of acting or not acting, and applies it to the shepherd who leads the flock to good pasture, watches there, and brings them back. He measures the abundance historically, as blessings greater than were ever enjoyed under the older dispensation, even in the promised land; and he is fiercest on the other side, that men who enter the ministry for its revenues are the basest of thieves, their doctrine deadly because it comes from no commission, adding that the charge is not to be applied to any one class of preachers only.

Chrysostom denies flatly that the prophets are meant, as he says the heretics take it, and names instead the agitators who had lately troubled the nation, supporting the reading from the next clause, since the sheep are praised for not hearing these men whereas those who disobeyed the prophets are everywhere condemned. Going in and out he refers to the apostles, who went in and out boldly and became the masters of the world, so that nobody could turn them out of their kingdom.

debates.question: Who are the all that ever came before him?

positions.position: Not the prophets, as heretics allege, but the agitators who had lately troubled the nation
Those who came unsent, and the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves, identified with the three shepherds cut off in one month
The scribes and Pharisees, since there is no evidence of any pretended Messiah before him, and all is used in its popular sense
Not Messianic pretenders, for hardly an instance of one can be found before that coming though many followed it, which is itself evidence of the timing

debates.question: What is promised in going in and out and finding pasture?

positions.position: The bold freedom of the apostles, whom nobody could turn out of their kingdom
A Hebrew idiom for the whole activity of a life and the liberty of acting or not acting
Freedom of access rather than range, the fold standing always open against storm or night

outliers.claim: Calls men who enter the ministry for its revenues the basest of thieves, their doctrine deadly because it carries no commission, while refusing to let the charge be fastened on any one class of preachers.
Reads the thief's design as the theft of affection rather than of property, carrying the sheep away from their shepherd as a rebel prince stole the hearts of a kingdom from his father.

themes: Then said Jesus unto them again, Verily, verily, I say unto you, I am the door of the sheep.
All that ever came before me are thieves and robbers: but the sheep did not hear them.
I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved, and shall go in and out, and find pasture.
The thief cometh not, but for to steal, and to kill, and to destroy: I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly.

11.pericope_label: I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep. But he that is an hireling, and not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, seeth the wolf coming, and leaveth the sheep, and fleeth: and the wolf catcheth them, and scattereth the sheep. The hireling fleeth, because he is an hireling, and careth not for the sheep. I am the good shepherd, and know my sheep, and am known of mine. As the Father knoweth me, even so know I the Father: and I lay down my life for the sheep.

schools.summary: Ellicott rules out the obvious target, the hierarchy having already been called thieves and robbers, and takes the word for anyone who enters the office from a motive other than love of men, or by any door but Christ, noting that the Greek implies something below a household servant; on the knowing he objects that the verse division obscures the sentence, which should run on so that the mutual knowledge of Father and Son is not a separate assertion but the measure of the union between shepherd and sheep. Barnes describes the hireling concretely, a minister who preaches for support, will run no risk, and would rather see the church wasted by its enemies than lose his reputation or place; and he says the word for knowing carries affectionate regard, pointing out that it is glossed by love a few verses later. Robertson keeps the proportion honest, that no one may claim a knowledge like that between Father and Son and yet the sheep really do know the voice and follow it in spite of thieves and hirelings.

Calvin declines the speculative question, how the Father knows his own Wisdom, and holds to what is said, that Christ stands between God and us as the bond of the union, so that it is no more possible for him to forget us than for the Father to disregard him.

Clarke's old English Bible gave him the word merchant, of one who makes merchandise of men's souls, and he sets the two figures against each other exactly: the hireling counts the sheep his own only so long as they are profitable to him, and the good shepherd counts them his own so long as he can be profitable to them. He adds a caution the others do not, that no reader should fasten this on one class of men, since every party may have its hireling and the danger is greatest where the provision is largest; and on the mutual knowledge he offers a parallel from Homer, goatherds separating their own beasts with ease though the flocks feed mixed together.
Chrysostom adds only what the last clause secures, that the passion was not undergone unwillingly.

Augustine takes up the difficulty the two images make together: if he is the door, how does he enter by himself? As he knows the Father by himself and we by him, so he enters the fold by himself and we by him, we coming in by the door because we preach Christ while Christ preaches himself, a light showing both other things and itself. From this he draws the limit on the office, that there is one Shepherd and the rulers of the Church who are sons and not hirelings are shepherds only as members of him, none of us calling himself the door; and he notes that good could not have been added unless there were bad shepherds too. The fault in the hireling he locates deeper than the wages, in a man who seeks in the Church not God but something else, where had he sought God he would be chaste. He also refuses to let suffering settle the question, since those who laid down their lives were good shepherds not because they shed their blood but because they shed it for the sheep.

positions.position: Not the hierarchy, already named thieves and robbers, but anyone entering the office from a motive other than love of men
The minister who preaches for support, will run no risk, and would rather see the church wasted than lose his place
One who seeks in the Church not God but something else, the fault lying deeper than the wages
The merchant who makes merchandise of souls, found in every party and likeliest where the provision is largest

debates.question: What kind of knowing passes between the shepherd and the sheep?

positions.position: Affectionate regard rather than information, the word being glossed by love a few verses later
Real but not commensurate, since no one may claim a knowledge like that between Father and Son
Not a separate assertion at all, the verse division obscuring a sentence in which the Father and Son's knowledge is the measure of the union
Left unspeculative, Christ standing between God and us as the bond of the union

outliers.claim: Refuses to let martyrdom settle who the good shepherd is, since blood may be shed in pride or against the sheep, and a body given to be burned without charity profits nothing.
Takes from the closing clause only the one security that matters to him, that the passion was not undergone unwillingly.

themes: I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.
But he that is an hireling, and not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, seeth the wolf coming, and leaveth the sheep, and fleeth: and the wolf catcheth them, and scattereth the sheep.
The hireling fleeth, because he is an hireling, and careth not for the sheep.
I am the good shepherd, and know my sheep, and am known of mine.
As the Father knoweth me, even so know I the Father: and I lay down my life for the sheep.

16.pericope_label: And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd. Therefore doth my Father love me, because I lay down my life, that I might take it again. No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. This commandment have I received of my Father.

schools.summary: Barnes refuses to let the present tense mean that these were already friends, and takes it for a purpose so settled that it could be spoken of as accomplished, comparing the assurance given at Corinth that God had much people in that city; the certainty, he presses, cannot rest on any disposition foreseen in them, since they were the most corrupt people of antiquity, so it must rest on the intention of God, from which he draws that salvation is no matter of chance and that a preacher has ground to expect success. On the one fold he keeps the historical edge, that this was a plain intimation of a gospel for the Gentiles, extremely offensive to those hearing it, and that no national privilege or pre-eminence of rank would remain. That the death was voluntary he argues from the escapes, and defends the right to it by ordinary cases, the patriot who dies on the field and the merchant who risks his life for gain. Ellicott calls the saying about the Father's love difficult and does not pretend otherwise, reading it of the self-devotion of the Son, so that he who gave his Son for the world loves the Son who of his own will gives himself, almost as though the salvation of mankind had called out a new relation of love between them; and he adds what most readers pass over, that the taking of the life again is given as part of the reason of that love.

Gill reads the clause of the elect among the Gentiles, sheep before they are called or folded, given to Christ and already in his hands. He spreads the Father's love wider, over the Son as Son from eternity, as Mediator, as clothed with our nature and as suffering in our room, and states the hard half plainly, that the bruising was a pleasure to the Father not in itself but because by it the counsel was accomplished. On the voluntary death he grants everything the history says, that the rulers procured it and the soldiers carried it out, and still holds that none of them could have taken it without the Father's will and his own consent.

Clarke hears the clause as an answer to something the hearers were about to think: they were not to imagine, when they saw him crucified, that he had been abandoned by his Father and so fallen into their hands, nor that he was put to death because he lacked the strength to resist.

Origen reaches the same point from the other end, taking the lamb led to the slaughter and the lamb standing as if slain, and finding in this very saying the proof that the one who led that lamb to the slaughter was God in man, the great High Priest.

debates.question: Why is the Father's love grounded on the laying down of the life?

positions.position: Because the self-devotion of the Son called out what is almost a new relation of love, the taking again being part of the reason given
Because the love is eternal and manifold, and the bruising pleased the Father not in itself but as the counsel accomplished
Because the clause forestalls the inference that the crucified one had been abandoned or simply overpowered

outliers.claim: Sets the lamb led to the slaughter beside the lamb standing as if slain, and finds in the saying itself the proof that the one who led that lamb was God in man, the great High Priest.
Defends the right to lay down one's life by ordinary cases, the patriot who dies on the field and the merchant who risks his life for gain.

themes: And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd.
Therefore doth my Father love me, because I lay down my life, that I might take it again.
No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. This commandment have I received of my Father.

19.pericope_label: There was a division therefore again among the Jews for these sayings. And many of them said, He hath a devil, and is mad; why hear ye him? Others said, These are not the words of him that hath a devil. Can a devil open the eyes of the blind?

schools.summary: Barnes says the same of preaching in general, that this teaching always produced an effect and made either bitter enemies or decided friends, as all faithful preaching will, so that the divisions are to be laid at the door of unbelief and not of the gospel. Ellicott takes the second clause of the accusation for an explanation of the first, the madness being simply what possession looks like, and identifies the speakers on the other side as the same moderate party in the council that had appeared once before. Robertson is brusque about the motive, that it was an easy way of discounting him and had been used before.

Gill supplies the background the others are working from, the Jewish notion of a particular evil spirit that takes away a man's understanding, and counts the numbers the other way about, the accusers many and the better sort few. Calvin reads the tactic as deliberate: the reproach is the most offensive one they can devise, chosen so that everybody may shudder at the thought of hearing him, and raised loudly enough that not a single word should be heard in silence; but the doctrine, he adds, has power enough in itself to answer such slanders.

Clarke insists that a demoniac and a madman were not the same thing to that people, and that the two terms are here distinguished rather than repeated: they held him possessed by a spirit which deranged his faculties, and inferred that he must have been a wicked man to be given over to such a spirit at all. He takes the defenders' argument seriously and completes it, since the words themselves are words of sense and sobriety, which is not how possession sounds, and beyond the words there is the fact that this man had opened the eyes of one born blind, which no demon does. From that he turns to the bearing of the accused, that not a word of impatience escaped him under such usage, and draws the practical conclusion for ministers, that a disciple should not expect better treatment than his master.

Henry takes the division as the expected result rather than an accident, the sayings having been fit to gather men round a common centre and instead setting them at odds, which is what had been foretold; and he notes drily that a congregation once split is not easily mended, rents being sooner made than made up. He will not treat the split as simply bad, since it is better that men should be divided about the doctrine of Christ than united in the service of sin. He hears two charges in the accusation and not one, the first falling on the speaker, since the worst of characters is regularly fastened on the best of men, and the second on the audience in the question why they listen at all. On the defenders he notices what it cost them, since the stream ran strong and they swam against it, and suspects that they did not believe him to be the Christ but simply could not bear to hear him abused.

debates.question: Is he hath a devil and is mad one charge or two?

positions.position: Two, distinguished: possession by a spirit that deranged him, and the wickedness inferred from his being given over to it
One, the second clause explaining the first, since madness is simply what possession looks like

debates.question: What was the accusation meant to accomplish?

positions.position: An easy way of discounting him, already used on an earlier occasion
The most offensive reproach available, raised loudly so that nobody should hear a word of his in silence
A double stroke, at the speaker's character and at the audience for listening at all

outliers.claim: Observes that men are ruined by being laughed out of their regard for the word, though they would never allow themselves to be laughed out of their food, which is less necessary.
Counts the parties the other way about from the commentators who dwell on the defenders, the accusers being many and the better sort few.

themes: There was a division therefore again among the Jews for these sayings.
And many of them said, He hath a devil, and is mad; why hear ye him?
Others said, These are not the words of him that hath a devil. Can a devil open the eyes of the blind?

22.pericope_label: And it was at Jerusalem the feast of the dedication, and it was winter. And Jesus walked in the temple in Solomon’s porch. Then came the Jews round about him, and said unto him, How long dost thou make us to doubt? If thou be the Christ, tell us plainly.

schools.summary: Barnes tells the story of the Maccabees, the city taken and thousands killed and sold, a sow sacrificed on the altar, the service suspended three years, then the purifying with eight days of hymns and gold crowns; he reads the note about winter as weather, cold and inclement and given expressly as the reason for the portico, and explains that the porch took Solomon's name not from being built by him but from standing where his porch had stood. Robertson notes that the term for the feast occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, that this was not one of the great feasts and could be observed anywhere, allows nearly three months for the interval and refuses a proposed rearrangement of the chapter as purely arbitrary. Ellicott puts the interval at about two months, cites a calculation dating the one feast to mid-October and this to the twentieth of December, and fills the gap from the third Gospel. Lightfoot is the only one who looks hard at the feast's other name, the feast of Lights, and will not accept the explanation offered for it, since one would suppose from the name that candles were lit and there is no mention of any.

Clarke tells the same story of the Maccabees and argues that there was no need to tell a reader it was winter when everyone knew the date, so that the word likelier means stormy or rainy, which explains the walking under cover. He observes that the evangelist passes over everything between the autumn feast and this one, probably because the others had covered it, and counts this the fourth of the four visits to Jerusalem that this Gospel alone records.

Henry makes a distinction about the kind of day it was: the celebration was not confined to Jerusalem, as the divinely appointed feasts were, but kept by every man in his own place, and kept not as a holy time, since only a divine institution can sanctify a day, but as a good time, like the days of Purim. He adds that Christ came up not in honour of a feast that did not require his attendance but to use the eight days of vacation, and that the council sat in the porch where he walked.

Chrysostom takes the feast for the dedication of the temple after the return from Babylon. On the question put to him he finds the perversity in the pattern, that when he teaches by discourse they demand a sign and when he demonstrates by works they demand a plain word, being determined to oppose either way; he hears malice in the phrase itself, since nothing had been hidden at the feasts, and takes the courteous preface for flattery meant to draw out something they could use.

Augustine supplies only the word, that any dedication of a new thing was called by the Greek name for new, and lets the season stand as a figure, the men who came being cold in love and burning in malevolence, and approaching not to honour but to persecute. On the question he says what they were angling for, a bare confession that he was the Christ, which men holding merely human notions of the Messiah could then turn into a charge of aspiring to a throne.

debates.question: Which dedication is the feast of the dedication?

positions.position: The dedication of the temple after the return from Babylon
The purifying under the Maccabees after the profanation, kept with eight days of hymns and gold crowns
Left unspecified, the name belonging to any dedication of a new thing

debates.question: Why does the evangelist remark that it was winter?

positions.position: For the weather rather than the calendar, the word likelier meaning stormy or rainy, since nobody needed telling the date
As cold and inclement, given expressly as the reason for walking in the portico
As a figure of the men who came, cold in love and burning in malevolence

outliers.claim: Presses the feast's other name and rejects the received explanation of it, since candles are nowhere mentioned and the rabbinic account of the eight days he calls a cunning way of talking about the matter.
Distinguishes a good time from a holy one, holding that only a divine institution can sanctify a day, so that this feast ranked with the days of Purim.

themes: And it was at Jerusalem the feast of the dedication, and it was winter.
And Jesus walked in the temple in Solomon’s porch.
Then came the Jews round about him, and said unto him, How long dost thou make us to doubt? If thou be the Christ, tell us plainly.

25.pericope_label: Jesus answered them, I told you, and ye believed not: the works that I do in my Father’s name, they bear witness of me. But ye believe not, because ye are not of my sheep, as I said unto you. My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me: And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand. My Father, which gave them me, is greater than all; and no man is able to pluck them out of my Father’s hand. I and my Father are one.

schools.summary: Barnes presses the original, which he renders as a declaration that they shall not be destroyed for ever, and notes that the verb for plucking means to rob, to seize and carry off as a robber does his prey, so that the picture is of an attempted theft that cannot succeed, the word any covering every power that might attempt it, man or devil, eloquent in error or mighty in rank. He draws the doctrine out in order and does not soften it, that the people are given by the Father to the Son, that the Son gives them the life which issues in glory, that Father and Son are alike pledged to keep them, and that no language could teach the perseverance of the saints more explicitly; then turns it into a test rather than a comfort. On the closing sentence he concedes what the grammar will not give him, since the word for one is neuter and expresses union without specifying its kind, and argues for a union of nature in four steps: the point in debate was power and not counsel, the hearers plainly understood a claim of equality, the speaker did not deny that this was his meaning, and he immediately said something else that produced the same effect. Ellicott notices the shape of the argument rather than its force, the thought mounting with each succeeding sentence, and refuses any limiting addition to the word all. Robertson stays with the manuscripts, where the readings differ between a masculine and a neuter both in the relative and in the comparative, and judges the neuter the likelier.

Gill reads the gift in the same direction, that the life given is already begun in a life of grace, held for them in their representative, and spoken of as given now because it is certain. On the closing sentence he reaches the same conclusion as Barnes by the grammar the others pass over, that the verb is plural, so that the sentence cannot mean one person but must mean one in nature and essence, and here particularly one in power, since the whole point at issue is whether the same hand holds the sheep.

Clarke keeps to the one clause about the Father's greatness, which he glosses as more powerful than all the united energies of men and demons, and draws from it the plainest of consequences, that whoever loves God must be happy, and whoever fears him need fear nothing on this side of eternity.

outliers.claim: Turns the promise of perseverance into a test rather than a comfort, since the only evidence anyone has of belonging to that flock is the persevering resignation of himself to God day after day.
Refuses any limiting addition to the word all in the Father is greater than all, extending it to every creature and every power, and even to the Son considered in his subordination to the Father.
Leaves the doctrine aside for the manuscripts, where relative and comparative alike vary between masculine and neuter, and judges the neuter the likelier reading.

themes: Jesus answered them, I told you, and ye believed not: the works that I do in my Father’s name, they bear witness of me.
But ye believe not, because ye are not of my sheep, as I said unto you.
My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me:
And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand.
My Father, which gave them me, is greater than all; and no man is able to pluck them out of my Father’s hand.
I and my Father are one.

31.pericope_label: Then the Jews took up stones again to stone him. Jesus answered them, Many good works have I shewed you from my Father; for which of those works do ye stone me? The Jews answered him, saying, For a good work we stone thee not; but for blasphemy; and because that thou, being a man, makest thyself God.

schools.summary: Barnes notes that these were the only works there were to appeal to, so that the appeal could be made confidently, and adds the reflection that it would be a happy thing if everyone under persecution could point his persecutors to such a record of his own innocence. Ellicott dissents about which quality of the works is in view, arguing that the word does not make their beneficence prominent but their moral excellence, and that no English word quite carries it, though excellent or distinguished come nearer than good; he notices too that the question uses a word marking quality rather than mere distinction, and that in the reply the preposition is not the causal one of the previous verse but the word proper to an indictment. Robertson reads the same reply as a piece of evasion, since taken literally it denies that any good deed had brought them to this, which flatly contradicts what had happened after the healing on the sabbath, and observes that the charge had been stated more accurately on an earlier occasion; he grants the fact at once and puts the only question that matters, that it was blasphemy only if he was not the Son of God.

Gill lists the good works as works of power that were also works of mercy, the sick healed, the possessed delivered, the lepers cleansed, the blind given sight. Calvin observes the constant habit behind the indictment, that wicked men carry on open war with God and still will not sin without first finding some plausible cover for it.

Clarke reaches the conclusion by a test of his own: had they understood no more than a unity of sentiment with the Father they would not have treated it as blasphemy at all, since in that sense Abraham and Moses and every prophet was one with God, and what enraged them was that they heard a unity of nature. He explains the idiom of showing good works, since in that language it means to do them in earnest and give good things liberally, and supports it from several psalms; and he distinguishes the two uses of the word for blasphemy, which applied to men means speaking injuriously of a person or character and applied to God means speaking impiously, contrary to his nature and perfections and the wisdom of his providence.

Chrysostom makes the same point from the reply rather than the offence, that the speaker did not correct them as men who had misheard him, but confirmed and defended what he had said in the very sense they had taken it.

Augustine puts the argument from the reaction most sharply, that the men who took up stones understood what a later party of interpreters did not, and were angry precisely because they could not take the words about being one with the Father as meaning anything short of equality.

debates.question: What shows that the hearers heard a claim of equality?

positions.position: Their anger, since men who took up stones could not have taken the words as meaning anything less
The reply, which confirmed and defended the saying in the sense they had taken it rather than correcting them
The charge of blasphemy itself, which a mere unity of sentiment could not have sustained, since in that sense every prophet was one with God

debates.question: Which quality of the works does for which of these works do ye stone me point to?

positions.position: Their beneficence, works of power that were works of mercy, shown in the idiom of dealing liberally
Not their beneficence but their moral excellence, which no English word quite carries

outliers.claim: Reads the reply as evasion, since taken literally it contradicts what followed the sabbath healing, and reduces the whole indictment to a single question, whether he was the Son of God.
Notices the habit rather than the argument, that wicked men carry on open war with God and still will not sin without first finding some plausible cover for it.

themes: Then the Jews took up stones again to stone him.
Jesus answered them, Many good works have I shewed you from my Father; for which of those works do ye stone me?
The Jews answered him, saying, For a good work we stone thee not; but for blasphemy; and because that thou, being a man, makest thyself God.

34.pericope_label: Jesus answered them, Is it not written in your law, I said, Ye are gods? If he called them gods, unto whom the word of God came, and the scripture cannot be broken; Say ye of him, whom the Father hath sanctified, and sent into the world, Thou blasphemest; because I said, I am the Son of God? If I do not the works of my Father, believe me not. But if I do, though ye believe not me, believe the works: that ye may know, and believe, that the Father is in me, and I in him.

schools.summary: Barnes notes that the word law here covers more than the books of Moses, since the sentence quoted comes from a psalm, and takes the gods of that psalm for magistrates, named so for the dignity of the office, remarking that such a use of the word is rare. He states with unusual care what the argument proves and what it does not: the clause that Scripture cannot be broken settles the authority of the text, so that if the word god is there applied to men in office its application to men is not in itself blasphemous; but the speaker did not deny that he meant the term of himself, nor that it was properly applied to him, nor that it implied he was God, affirming only that his accusers were inconsistent. Sanctified he insists cannot mean made holy, since the Son was always holy, and takes it for setting apart from a common to a sacred use. Ellicott adds that the pronoun is emphatic in both Hebrew and Greek and reads the psalm as God sitting in judgment on the judges he had appointed and giving them a name that represents himself; he fixes the consecration on a moment instead, the Messianic work and the Incarnation which began it, and on the appeal to the works he is gentler and more exacting at once, holding that a higher faith would have believed the speaker himself and preferring a reading which asks them to perceive first and then to know permanently. Lightfoot reports what the rabbis had made of the same verse, calls it a most ridiculous sense, and sets against it the reading he thinks the whole contexture of the psalm requires, that it speaks of the magistracy, to whom the word of God came as an express commission and warrant for governing.

Gill puts the act of sanctifying far earlier, in the eternal separation of the Son to the work of Mediator before the foundation of the world, and argues that this presupposes his eternal existence and so proves his deity by implication.

Clarke agrees that the word law reaches beyond Moses, says the same of the judges called gods, and thinks this probably the only place in the Hebrew where the word is applied to any but the true God. He calls the reasoning from the works conclusive, since the only way to weaken it was to deny that the miracles were wrought by the power of God, which would have obliged the accusers to maintain that a bad man could work them, so that the argument had a complete triumph.

debates.question: What does sanctified and sent into the world mean?

positions.position: Setting apart from a common to a sacred use, the consecration of a man to an office, since the Son was always holy
The eternal separation of the Son to the work of Mediator before the foundation of the world
The consecration to the Messianic work and the Incarnation which began it

debates.question: How strong is the closing appeal to the works?

positions.position: Conclusive and a complete triumph, since the only escape was to maintain that a bad man could work such miracles
A lower ground taken only because a higher faith failed, perception of the works being the step up to permanent knowledge
Simply that none could do them unless sent from God, the union asserted being possible in no other case

outliers.claim: Reports and then demolishes the rabbinic reading of the psalm, that but for the sin with the calf the fathers would have been like angels and begotten no children, calling it a most ridiculous sense.
Lists what the speaker declined to deny: that he meant the term of himself, that it was properly applied to him, and that it implied he was God.

themes: Jesus answered them, Is it not written in your law, I said, Ye are gods?
If he called them gods, unto whom the word of God came, and the scripture cannot be broken;
Say ye of him, whom the Father hath sanctified, and sent into the world, Thou blasphemest; because I said, I am the Son of God?
If I do not the works of my Father, believe me not.
But if I do, though ye believe not me, believe the works: that ye may know, and believe, that the Father is in me, and I in him.

39.pericope_label: Therefore they sought again to take him: but he escaped out of their hand, And went away again beyond Jordan into the place where John at first baptized; and there he abode. And many resorted unto him, and said, John did no miracle: but all things that John spake of this man were true. And many believed on him there.

schools.summary: Barnes turns the retreat into a general observation, that the persecution was itself the occasion of the journey, so that the wrath of men was made to serve the cause they opposed; on the place he agrees with Lightfoot, and on what the people said of the Baptist he points out the form of their reasoning, that John gave no miracle but foretold the character and the success of the one who came after, and that either a miracle or a prophecy is conclusive proof of a mission. Ellicott works the geography out at length and settles on a place north of the lake on the eastern side, then reads the withdrawal as a turning point, the teaching by divine words having been answered with stones and the appeal to divine works with an attempted arrest, so that the retirement from the city leaves it unvisited until the last Passover; yet he refuses to let the chapter end in the dark, since the light is never wholly absent, and sets the reception on the old ground against the rejection at the capital. He also makes the Baptist's want of signs a kind of evidence, since the man who did no sign had recognised the glory further than anyone else of his generation. Lightfoot answers a different question, identifying the spot by the earlier narrative as the Bethabara where the baptising began.

Gill draws a distinction in the attempt, that this was not the furious stoning of a moment earlier but a design to lay hold of him and bring him before the council, which is a different and colder intention.

Clarke denies that the phrase means the far bank at all and would render it to the side of Jordan rather than beyond it. He puts the two grounds of the people's belief in order, the testimony of a man they knew to be honest and a prophet, and the miracles they had seen for themselves; then draws a comparison, that the scribes and Pharisees with all their learning could not reach a conclusion so plain, and that truth and common sense are often found with ordinary people whom the insolently wise are willing enough to dismiss as a mob.
Bede marks the persistence rather than the escape, that they were still in the same madness and tried once more to seize him.

debates.question: Where is the place beyond Jordan to which he withdrew?

positions.position: Not the far bank at all, the phrase meaning to the side of Jordan rather than beyond it
The eastern side, north of the lake, the province proper lying west of the river and the name having spread eastward
The Bethabara of the earlier narrative, identified from the record rather than from the geography

outliers.claim: Marks the persistence rather than the escape, that the same madness held them and they tried once more to seize him.
Refuses to let the withdrawal read as an ending, taking it for the darkness before night while holding to the note struck in the Gospel's opening words, that the light is never wholly absent.

themes: Therefore they sought again to take him: but he escaped out of their hand,
And went away again beyond Jordan into the place where John at first baptized; and there he abode.
And many resorted unto him, and said, John did no miracle: but all things that John spake of this man were true.
And many believed on him there.
